rendered:
Best retention after 200 cycles[1] at 0.5C[2]: LLTO-2, which kept 86.2%[3] of its initial discharge capacity. This is just above LLTO-0.5 (85.5%[4]) and far above LLTO-1 (57.2%[5]). By comparison, the pristine NCM only retained 56.6% of its initial discharge capacity after 200 cycles[6], so the best LLTO coating kept a much larger share of its capacity. The LLTO coating also left the initial capacity almost unchanged: the paper says the LLTO coated NCM exhibited almost similar[7] initial discharge capacity compared to pristine NC-622 material, while its rate capability was better: LLTO coated NCM materials exhibited improved rate capability[8]. The paper credits this to the ionic conductivity of the LLTO coating layer[9] and to suppressed side reactions with the electrolyte.

Why the 2 mol.%[10] coating lowered rate capability: the paper gives the reason as the coating getting thicker. It says the rate capability decreased, which may be due to the thickness of the coating layer, resulting in the suppression of electron[11] transfer process during charge/discharge cycling. So the thicker layer is thought to block electron transfer, even though the same coating gave the best cycling retention. The text does not give numeric rate-capability values; those are only shown in the rate-capability panel of the figure.
